title: Erie Well Depth and Drilling Cost
meta_description: Erie wells have a 50-foot median depth, 10 gpm median yield, and typical finished costs of $8,500-$15,500.
h1: What Erie, Colorado Wells Are Really Like
intro_html:
If you are buying land or a home in Erie, the nearby well records give a useful starting point. Within five miles, Colorado DWR records show 2,507 permitted wells. Reported depths range from shallow plains wells to a deepest record of 1,282 feet, but the typical well is much shallower: the median is 50 feet.

These records include domestic, stock, irrigation, and monitoring wells, so they are not a guarantee for one particular lot. Still, the yield and static-water-level data are generally favorable. The important work is matching nearby records to your parcel, confirming the permit, and budgeting for the ground conditions and site work that apply there.

sections.heading: Erie well depths vary sharply across the plains
sections.html:
The median reported well depth near Erie is 50 feet. The middle half runs from 24 to 250 feet, which is a wide spread for a drilling estimate. About 62% of reported wells are under 100 feet, while 16% fall between 100 and 300 feet, 15% between 300 and 600 feet, and 7% exceed 600 feet. The deepest record is 1,282 feet.

That spread matters when reviewing a driller's bid. A nearby shallow well can be encouraging, but it does not prove your lot will match it. Erie sits over Denver Basin sedimentary bedrock, and the aquifer named on every listed well is a Denver Basin aquifer. Nearby records in Leyner, Lafayette, Dacono, Frederick, Broomfield, and Gunbarrel can add context, but the closest comparable wells are the most useful.

sections.heading: Most Erie wells report a workable household yield
sections.html:
Among the wells with a reported pump yield, the median is 10.0 gallons per minute. The middle half runs from 9.0 to 14.0 gallons per minute. Seventy-two percent report yields from 5 to 15 gallons per minute, and 24% report more than 15 gallons per minute. No reported well is under 1 gallon per minute, while 3% fall between 1 and 5 gallons per minute.

That is a solid local record for ordinary household use, but only 230 wells report a pump yield. A yield number is not the same as storage in the well or guaranteed pressure at the house. Ask for the completion report and pumping information for nearby domestic wells. An exempt household-use well is still subject to its permit terms and the applicable Colorado limits.

sections.heading: Erie water levels are relatively shallow in the records
sections.html:
The reported static water level has a median depth of 12 feet below ground surface, with the middle half from 7 to 27 feet. That suggests water is commonly encountered fairly close to the surface in the available records. It can reduce pumping lift, but it also means shallow groundwater may be more exposed to surface conditions if a well is poorly constructed or a site is poorly managed.

The decade figures do not show a dropping trend in this dataset. The median measured water level was 18 feet below surface in the 2010s and 10 feet in the 2020s, meaning the later reported measurements are shallower. Only 90 wells report a static water level, so treat that comparison as a record summary, not a basin-wide forecast for your property.

sections.heading: Erie has a long permit history and several recurring drillers
sections.html:
Permits appear throughout the record, with 43 issued in the 1950s, 77 in the 1960s, 284 in the 1970s, 209 in the 1980s, 284 in the 1990s, 231 in the 2000s, 310 in the 2010s, and 303 in the 2020s. The newest permit year is 2026. That history shows sustained well development around Erie rather than a small, isolated group of permits.

The most frequent driller entry is Authorized (Pe, Pg), followed by Waneka & Son Drilling and Ground Water Systems Inc. Those names identify patterns in the permit records, not a recommendation. Of the 2,507 permits, 1,268 are recorded as constructed, 1,372 report depth, and only 230 report pump yield. Check the actual permit and construction report for any property under contract.

sections.heading: What drilling a well costs near Erie
sections.html:
For Erie’s Denver Basin sedimentary bedrock, the drilling rate model is typically $50 to $70 per foot. At the 50-foot median depth, the drilled hole works out to about $2,500 to $3,500. That is only the hole. A finished well with pump, pressure tank, trenching, and electrical is estimated at about $8,500 to $15,500.

The final bid can move outside that range because depth, casing and grout, access, trench length, power requirements, and site layout are property-specific. A shallow neighboring well is useful evidence, not a fixed price. Have a driller review the permit records and inspect access before relying on a drilling allowance in a purchase contract or construction budget.

sections.heading: Check contamination, construction, and septic constraints
sections.html:
Mapped environmental records within about ten miles include 950 PFAS sampling or contamination sites, 61 historic mine features, and 20 EPA Superfund or cleanup sites. A map point does not automatically mean a particular parcel’s well water is unsafe, but it is a reason to order a well-water test and investigate the site history. Pay attention to the well’s casing, grout, cap, and location relative to drainage and waste systems.

Low yield is not the main pattern in the reported Erie records, but dry holes and poor construction remain possible on an individual lot. Septic setbacks, replacement-area requirements, access for drilling equipment, and the location of the house, driveway, and utility trenches should be reviewed together. Water rights also matter: confirm the permit allows the intended household, livestock, or irrigation use before closing.

sections.heading: Use the nearby records before buying or building
sections.html:
Start with the exact parcel, then compare the closest constructed wells by depth, aquifer, use, yield, and static water level. The overall Erie median is encouraging, but the 24-to-250-foot middle range shows why a single nearby record should not set your expectations. A licensed driller can assess access and give a better site-specific allowance after reviewing those records.

For a home purchase, make the well permit, construction report, pump equipment, and water test part of the investigation. For a new build, place the well, septic system, house, and driveway as one site plan rather than solving each later. The same review applies around Leyner, Lafayette, Dacono, Frederick, Broomfield, and Gunbarrel, where conditions may differ from the closest Erie parcel.

faq.q: How deep are wells in Erie, Colorado?
faq.a: The median reported well depth within five miles of Erie is 50 feet. The middle half runs from 24 to 250 feet, 62% are under 100 feet, and the deepest record is 1,282 feet. Those figures include different well uses and do not guarantee the depth on a particular parcel.

faq.q: How much does it cost to drill a well in Erie, Colorado?
faq.a: The local cost model uses $50 to $70 per foot for Denver Basin sedimentary bedrock. At the 50-foot median depth, the drilled hole is about $2,500 to $3,500. A finished well with pump, tank, trenching, and electrical is estimated at $8,500 to $15,500.

faq.q: How much water do wells produce in Erie?
faq.a: Reported pump yields have a 10.0 gallon-per-minute median, with the middle half from 9.0 to 14.0 gallons per minute. Seventy-two percent report 5 to 15 gallons per minute. Only 230 wells report yield, so review the closest domestic completion and pumping records before relying on the local median.

faq.q: Is well water safe in Erie, Colorado?
faq.a: The well records do not establish that water is safe to drink. Within about ten miles, mapped records include 950 PFAS sampling or contamination sites, 61 historic mine features, and 20 EPA Superfund or cleanup sites. Test the specific well, review nearby environmental history, and inspect casing, grout, and the well location.

faq.q: Is the water table dropping near Erie, Colorado?
faq.a: The available decade summary does not show a dropping trend. Median reported static water level was 18 feet below surface in the 2010s and 10 feet in the 2020s, so later measurements were shallower. Only 90 wells report static water level, making this a limited record summary rather than a forecast for every Erie property.
